subjective.question: Define an experiment, a treatment, an experimental unit and a factor.
subjective.answer: Illustrate each with an example. An experiment is a planned inquiry in which the investigator deliberately applies certain conditions (treatments) to experimental material and records the responses, in order to draw valid conclusions about the treatments. A treatment is a specific condition or procedure applied to an experimental unit, e.g. a particular dose of a fertilizer or a teaching method. An experimental unit is the smallest unit of experimental material to which a treatment is applied independently, e.g. a plot of land, a patient, or a group of students. A factor is a controlled independent variable whose different categories (levels) give rise to the treatments; for example, if three varieties of wheat are compared, 'variety' is the factor and each variety is a treatment. In the teaching example, the different teaching methods are the treatments and the groups of students are the experimental units.

subjective.question: What is meant by design and analysis of experiments?
subjective.answer: State its main objectives. Design and analysis of experiments is the branch of statistics concerned with planning an experiment so that appropriate data are obtained, and with drawing valid inferences from those data with respect to the problem under investigation. Its main objectives are: (i) to obtain maximum information with minimum resources (time, money and material); (ii) to reduce the experimental error so that genuine treatment differences can be detected; (iii) to provide a valid estimate of the experimental error for testing the significance of treatment effects; and (iv) to ensure that the conclusions drawn are reliable and applicable to the conditions represented by the experimental material.

subjective.question: Explain the three basic principles of experimental design: replication, randomization and local control.
subjective.answer: Replication means repeating each treatment on two or more experimental units. It provides an estimate of the experimental error and increases the precision of the experiment by reducing the standard error of a treatment mean. Randomization is the random allocation of treatments to experimental units, usually with the help of a random numbers table. It removes bias and the sources of extraneous variation, and it justifies the assumptions (independence of errors) on which the statistical analysis rests. Local control is the amount of balancing, blocking and grouping of the experimental units adopted in the design to reduce the experimental error; units are grouped into homogeneous blocks so that comparisons among treatments are made within nearly uniform material.

subjective.question: What is experimental error?
subjective.answer: Discuss its main sources. Experimental error is the variation among the responses of experimental units that receive the same treatment. It is the part of the total variation that cannot be attributed to treatments. Its main sources are: (i) natural variation among the experimental units (e.g. inherent differences in fertility of plots or ability of subjects); (ii) extraneous factors that are not controlled during the experiment, such as changes in temperature, humidity or handling; (iii) the joint effect (interaction) of the treatments and the experimental units; and (iv) errors of observation and measurement. A good experimental design aims to minimize and properly estimate this error so that treatment effects can be tested against it.

subjective.question: Define a Completely Randomized Design (CRD). When is it suitable, and what are its advantages and disadvantages?
subjective.answer: In a Completely Randomized Design, the treatments are allocated to the experimental units entirely at random, with no grouping or restriction, so that every unit has an equal chance of receiving any treatment. It is suitable when the experimental units are homogeneous, as in laboratory experiments, and when some units may fail so that unequal replications result. Advantages: it is the simplest design; it allows any number of treatments and unequal replications; the analysis remains simple even with missing observations; and it gives the maximum degrees of freedom for error. Disadvantages: if the units are heterogeneous, the experimental error becomes large and the design is the least efficient, because all the variation among units goes into the error.

subjective.question: State the linear model for a Completely Randomized Design and give its ANOVA skeleton with degrees of freedom.
subjective.answer: The linear model for a CRD with k treatments, the i-th treatment replicated nᵢ times, is: Yᵢⱼ = μ + τᵢ + εᵢⱼ, where Yᵢⱼ is the observation on the j-th unit receiving the i-th treatment, μ is the general mean, τᵢ is the effect of the i-th treatment and εᵢⱼ is the random error, assumed independent with mean zero and constant variance σ². The null hypothesis is H₀: τ₁ = τ₂ = ... = τₖ = 0 (all treatment means equal), against the alternative that not all treatment means are equal. ANOVA skeleton: Treatments — df k−1, SS = SSTr, MS = MSTr = SSTr/(k−1); Error — df n−k, SS = SSE, MS = MSE = SSE/(n−k); Total — df n−1, SS = SST, where n is the total number of observations. The test statistic is F = MSTr/MSE.

subjective.question: Define a Randomized Complete Block Design (RCBD). How is it an improvement over the CRD?
subjective.answer: In a Randomized Complete Block Design, the experimental material is divided into groups (blocks) of homogeneous units, the number of units in each block being equal to the number of treatments. Each block contains every treatment exactly once, and the treatments are assigned to the units within a block at random, independently in each block. RCBD improves on the CRD by local control: because comparisons among treatments are made within homogeneous blocks, the variation due to the heterogeneity of the material (e.g. a fertility gradient) is separated out as the block sum of squares instead of inflating the experimental error. The result is a smaller error mean square, a more precise experiment, and greater efficiency when the units are heterogeneous.

subjective.question: State the linear model for RCBD and give its ANOVA skeleton with degrees of freedom.
subjective.answer: The linear model for an RCBD with k treatments and r blocks is: Yᵢⱼ = μ + τᵢ + βⱼ + εᵢⱼ, where Yᵢⱼ is the observation on the i-th treatment in the j-th block, μ is the general mean, τᵢ is the i-th treatment effect, βⱼ is the j-th block effect and εᵢⱼ is the random error. In this design the total variation is decomposed into Treatments, Blocks and Error. ANOVA skeleton: Treatments — df k−1; Blocks — df r−1; Error — df (k−1)(r−1); Total — df kr−1. The treatment effect is tested by F = MSTr/MSE. For example, with 7 treatments and 4 blocks, the error degrees of freedom are (7−1)(4−1) = 18.

subjective.question: How is a missing observation in an RCBD estimated?
subjective.answer: Illustrate the effect of one missing observation on the error degrees of freedom and the mean square error. When one observation is missing in an RCBD, it is estimated by the value that minimizes the error sum of squares (Yates' formula): x = [k·B + r·T − G] / [(k−1)(r−1)], where k is the number of treatments, r the number of blocks, B is the total of the known observations in the block containing the missing unit, T is the total of the known observations of the treatment containing the missing unit, and G is the grand total of all known observations. The estimated value is inserted, the analysis proceeds as usual, but one degree of freedom is deducted from the error (and total) degrees of freedom. Define a Latin Square Design (LSD).
subjective.answer: State its conditions and give the degrees of freedom in its ANOVA for a k × k square. A Latin Square Design is an experimental design in which the experimental units are arranged in a square with k rows and k columns, and each of the k treatments occurs once and only once in each row and in each column. It controls variation in two directions (rows and columns) simultaneously. Conditions: the number of treatments must equal the number of rows and the number of columns; it is most practical for a moderate number of treatments (about 5 to 12). The number of distinct squares that can be formed by permuting the rows and columns of a k × k square is k!(k−1)!. ANOVA degrees of freedom: Rows k−1; Columns k−1; Treatments k−1; Error (k−1)(k−2); Total k²−1. The error sum of squares is obtained as SSE = SST − SSTr − SSR − SSC.

subjective.question: What is meant by the relative efficiency of RCBD over CRD?
subjective.answer: Give its formula and explain how it is interpreted. The relative efficiency of the RCBD relative to the CRD measures how many times more (or less) efficient the blocked design is than the completely randomized design for the same material. It is computed as: RE(RCBD, CRD) = Estimated MSE for the CR design / MSE for the RCBD, where the numerator is the error mean square that would have been obtained had the same material been laid out as a CRD, estimated from the block and error mean squares of the RCBD. If RE > 1, blocking has gained precision and the RCBD is more efficient than the CRD; if RE ≈ 1, blocking was of little use; if RE < 1, the CRD would have been better. An RE of, say, 1.5 means the CRD would need about 50% more replications to achieve the same precision as the RCBD.

subjective.question: Give the formulae for the efficiency of a Latin Square Design relative to RCBD and state when the LSD is preferred.
subjective.answer: When the rows of the Latin square are taken as blocks of an RCBD, the efficiency of the LSD relative to that RCBD is: E = (1/k) [ (sc²/se²) + (k − 1) ], where sc² is the column mean square and se² is the error mean square of the Latin square. When the columns are taken as blocks, the efficiency is: E = (1/k) [ (sr²/se²) + (k − 1) ], where sr² is the row mean square. A value greater than 1 indicates that the Latin square is more efficient than the corresponding RCBD because it additionally removes the variation in the second direction. The LSD is preferred when the experimental material varies in two perpendicular directions (e.g. two fertility gradients in a field) and the number of treatments is moderate, so that both sources of variation can be controlled at once.

subjective.question: State the assumptions underlying the analysis of variance (ANOVA).
subjective.answer: The analysis of variance rests on the following assumptions about the random errors εᵢⱼ in the linear model: (i) Additivity — the treatment, block and error effects combine additively, so the observation is the sum of the general mean, the relevant effects and error; (ii) Independence — the errors are independent of one another, which is ensured in practice by randomization; (iii) Normality — the errors are normally distributed with mean zero; and (iv) Homogeneity of variance — the errors have a common constant variance σ² for all treatments. In particular, the observations themselves must be independent for the F-test to be valid. If these assumptions are badly violated, the conclusions of the ANOVA may be misleading and a transformation of the data or a non-parametric method should be considered.

subjective.question: Distinguish between CRD, RCBD and Latin Square Design.
subjective.answer: The three designs differ in the extent of local control they apply. In a CRD there is no grouping at all: treatments are randomized over all units, so it is appropriate only for homogeneous material, and the error has n−k degrees of freedom. In an RCBD the units are grouped into homogeneous blocks in one direction; each block contains all treatments, variation between blocks is removed from the error, and the error degrees of freedom are (k−1)(r−1). In a Latin Square Design the units are grouped in two directions, as rows and columns of a k × k square; each treatment appears once in every row and column, variation in both directions is removed from the error, and the error degrees of freedom are (k−1)(k−2). Thus the LSD controls the most variation but is restricted to a square layout with equal numbers of treatments, rows and columns, whereas the CRD is the most flexible and the RCBD lies in between.
